title: Proof pages for a fintech product
metaTitle: Fintech product case study page structure
excerpt: A fintech proof page should show the constraint, the decision, and the product with the people responsible, then tell a similar buyer how to start.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground, two traces a reader can follow, for a proof page that has to show a decision rather than a blur.
caption: Blue and orange ink on white. Proof should leave a trace a buyer can follow. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a fintech case study include?
faqs.answer: Include the constraint the customer had, the decision you made, and the product state that resulted, with the people who were responsible. Leave out the tour of every screen. A buyer who may trust you with money is looking for judgment under a limit, not a gallery.

faqs.question: Can we publish a case study without the customer's name?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the situation is still specific and true. Describe the kind of company, the constraint, and the decision without inventing a name or a result. A named customer is stronger when you have permission. An unnamed story that stays concrete is stronger than a logo with no story at all.

faqs.question: How should a proof page end?
faqs.answer: End by telling a similar buyer how to start an account or talk to sales, and what to bring so the conversation starts from their constraint. Do not end on a slogan. The last sentence should be a path that matches the story they just read.

markdown:
A fintech product case study page should show the constraint, the decision, and the product with the people responsible for it. A buyer who may trust you with money is reading for judgment. Screenshots without a decision are decoration.

End on a path. Tell a similar buyer how to start an account or talk to sales. A proof page that concludes with "the future of finance" has forgotten why the reader stayed.

## Start with the constraint

The constraint is the reason the story exists. A marketplace could not pay sellers without a weekly spreadsheet. A platform's bank partner would not support a new country. A finance lead could not explain a hold to a customer without exporting three systems. Write that limit in the first paragraph, in the customer's words.

Google's notes on how content is created use product evidence as a trust signal: what was examined, what the result was, and photographs of the work. A case study is that shape, even when you are not reviewing gadgets. Name the limit you actually worked inside. A story with no constraint is an advertisement. Readers who have money at stake have learned to skip advertisements.

Be precise about what kind of customer this was. Stage, rough volume band if you can say it honestly, countries, and who inside their company felt the pain. "A leading fintech" is not a kind of customer. "A marketplace with sellers in two countries and a finance team of three" is. If you cannot say the band, say the shape. Do not invent a figure to make the opening sound researched.

Put the buyer's risk in the constraint. Not your team's inconvenience. The reader is deciding whether you understand what can go wrong with money. A late file is an inconvenience. A seller who cannot pay rent because a payout is invisible is the risk. Write the version you are allowed to write. Do not dramatize beyond the facts you have.

## Show the decision, including what you refused

The middle of the page is the decision. What you chose, what you declined, and why. This is the part most proof pages replace with a process diagram. A diagram of "discover, define, deliver" is your method. The buyer wants the fork in the road.

Useful decisions on a money product:

- You settled to an existing bank instead of asking the customer to open a new one.
- You left card issuing out of scope so payouts could launch.
- You put a human review on holds above a threshold rather than automating every exception.
- You refused a corridor you could not support, and the customer stayed for the corridor you could.

Write the refusal in the same size type as the win. A proof page that only lists additions teaches the reader you will say yes to everything. The boundary is the proof. It should sound like the boundary on your services page. If the story contradicts the public boundary, fix one of them before you publish.

Name the person, on your side and on theirs, who made the call. "We decided" is weaker than "their finance lead and our operations owner agreed to keep holds visible in the ledger." Accountability is the product you are selling, whether or not the page uses that word.

## Put the product and the people in the same story

Show the product in the state the story is about. The hold, the payout, the export, the exception queue. Crop to the decision. A full marketing screenshot with fake confetti numbers undermines the paragraph above it. If you must blur a balance, blur it, and do not replace it with a flattering fiction.

Pair the screen with the person responsible. A caption can do this in one sentence. "The hold view their support lead uses when a seller writes in." The reader should see that a human and an interface share the job. A gallery of UI with no operator, or a portrait with no product, splits the proof into two weaker pages.

Got Next and Leadly, public Hanabi product interfaces, are examples of screens edited down to a job. Use that standard on the case study even when the domain is money. One screen. The state that matters. Words that say what a person does next. If you need six screens, you are touring the product. Move the tour to the product page. Keep one or two frames here.

Alt text should describe the frame. "Payout list filtered to failed transfers" is alt text. "Best fintech platform" is a keyword stuffed into an image, and it fails the reader who cannot see the picture. The caption can carry the decision the alt text should not editorialize.

## Numbers you can stand behind

Use a number only when you can explain where it came from and the customer agrees. Time to reconciliation, share of payouts that no longer need a file, tickets about missing payouts. One number, with the before and the after defined the same way, is enough.

Do not borrow a vanity metric. "10x faster" with no baseline is a slogan. "The Friday file dropped from a half day of work to a check of exceptions" is a result a peer can imagine. If you do not have the measurement, write the qualitative result and stop. An honest gap is safer than a precise fiction, especially on a financial topic where Google's own guidance treats trust as the point of expertise signals.

Avoid percentages that your contract says you cannot publish. A proof page is not the place to leak a customer's volume. When in doubt, describe the direction and the mechanism. "Failed payouts became visible the same day, because the ledger showed the bank response instead of a generic error." That sentence can be enough.

If the result is mixed, say so. "Payouts improved. Chargeback handling stayed manual." Mixed results make the decision credible. A page where every metric improved by a round number reads as a template. Careful buyers notice the roundness.

## Structure the page so it can be quoted

A proof page should be easy to cite in a sales conversation and in a search snippet. Use a short title that names the constraint, not "Case study 04." Open with two sentences a stranger could read aloud. Then the decision. Then the product. Then the limit of the result. Then the path.

A simple shape:

1. Who the customer was, and the constraint.
2. The decision, including a refusal.
3. The product state and the person responsible.
4. What changed, in words you can defend.
5. Who this story is not for.
6. How a similar buyer starts.

"Who this is not for" keeps the story from being misread as a universal promise. If the approach depended on a single entity in one country, say that. A buyer who does not fit can leave without a call. That saves both of you. It also makes the buyers who do fit more confident that you know the edges.

Keep the writing plain. Defined terms can be introduced once. Do not make the reader learn your brand language to understand a payout. The page is a record of a job. Records are specific and a little dry. Dry is a compliment here.

## End on the path for a similar buyer

The last section is practical. If the reader recognizes their constraint, what do they do? Start an account, and here is what the application will ask. Or talk to sales, and here is what to send first: countries, roughly how money moves today, and the failure they want to stop. The ask should be short because the page has already done the explaining.

Do not introduce a new offer in the last paragraph. If the story was about payouts, the path is about payouts. A sudden pitch for a card product feels like the story was bait. Link the related service by its job name if they might need it later. Do not change the subject.

Invite a conversation only when a person will actually have it. "Book a call" that lands in an unattended inbox is a broken proof page. Say who reads the note and what happens next. A reply that confirms fit, or a clear no, is a respectable ending. Promise only what your team does.

Hanabi's work on proof is the same discipline as the rest of a site: a constraint, a decision, and a thing a stranger can see. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) covers that kind of page when you want it designed and built with the product story, not pasted on afterward.

## Keep a proof page from going stale

Date the story in ordinary language. "This describes the payout flow as it worked in the season we shipped it." If the product has changed, update the screen or mark the difference. A case study that shows a retired interface teaches the buyer your site is a museum.

Re-read the page when the customer relationship changes. Permission can be withdrawn. A number can stop being true. Assign a person, not a committee, to that review. The same person should be allowed to unpublish. A live page you no longer believe is worse than a gap in the work section.

Store the approved facts with the page. The constraint, the decision, the permitted numbers, the screenshot source. On a Hanabi project those notes live in the client portal with the other docs, so the next edit does not rely on someone's memory of what the customer allowed. The public page stays short. The record of permission stays findable.

Navigation is the next problem, because a proof page that no one can find is a private document. [Navigation for a fintech product](/blog/navigation-for-a-fintech-product) is about labeling the jobs a buyer already has words for, including the path into a story like this.
